claim: Oxytocin is produced by magnocellular neurons of the paraventricular (PVN) and supraoptic nuclei (SON) of the hypothalamus.
source: Oxytocin (Oxt) is produced by magnocellular neurons of the paraventricular (PVN) and supraoptic nuclei (SON) of the hypothalamus and released into the bloodstream from posterior pituitary nerve terminals.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about oxytocin production and is stated directly in the manuscript.

claim: Oxytocin is released into the bloodstream from posterior pituitary nerve terminals.
source: Oxytocin (Oxt) is produced by magnocellular neurons of the paraventricular (PVN) and supraoptic nuclei (SON) of the hypothalamus and released into the bloodstream from posterior pituitary nerve terminals.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about oxytocin release and is stated directly in the manuscript.

claim: Oxytocin activates G protein-coupled Oxt receptors (Oxtr) in peripheral target tissues.
source: By activating G protein-coupled Oxt receptors (Oxtr) in peripheral target tissues, Oxt exerts multiple effects, most prominently uterine contraction during parturition and milk ejection after delivery.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about oxytocin receptor activation and is stated directly in the manuscript.

claim: Oxytocin exerts uterine contraction during parturition.
source: By activating G protein-coupled Oxt receptors (Oxtr) in peripheral target tissues, Oxt exerts multiple effects, most prominently uterine contraction during parturition and milk ejection after delivery.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about oxytocin's physiological effects and is stated directly in the manuscript.

claim: Oxytocin exerts milk ejection after delivery.
source: By activating G protein-coupled Oxt receptors (Oxtr) in peripheral target tissues, Oxt exerts multiple effects, most prominently uterine contraction during parturition and milk ejection after delivery.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about oxytocin's physiological effects and is stated directly in the manuscript.

claim: Oxytocin is released in the brain by synaptic release from projections of parvocellular PVN neurons.
source: In addition, Oxt is released in the brain by synaptic release from projections of parvocellular PVN neurons and by hormone-like release from the somata and dendrites of magnocellular neurons (Ludwig and Leng, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ludwig and Leng, 2006.

claim: Oxytocin is released in the brain by hormone-like release from the somata and dendrites of magnocellular neurons.
source: In addition, Oxt is released in the brain by synaptic release from projections of parvocellular PVN neurons and by hormone-like release from the somata and dendrites of magnocellular neurons (Ludwig and Leng, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ludwig and Leng, 2006.

claim: Oxytocin can act in diverse Oxtr-expressing brain areas even when direct innervation by Oxt-containing fibers is absent.
source: Based on these processes and its long half-life, Oxt can act in diverse Oxtr-expressing brain areas even when direct innervation by Oxt-containing fibers is absent (Stoop, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stoop, 2012 and is based on inference from oxytocin's release mechanisms and half-life.

claim: Oxytocin promotes facial recognition.
source: Key regulatory effects of Oxt on animal and human behavior include promotion of facial recognition and maternal nurturing (Ferguson et al., 2001, 2000), control of anxiety (Bale et al., 2001; Yoshida et al., 2009), and regulation of spatial memory (Tomizawa et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ferguson et al., 2001, 2000.

claim: Oxytocin promotes maternal nurturing.
source: Key regulatory effects of Oxt on animal and human behavior include promotion of facial recognition and maternal nurturing (Ferguson et al., 2001, 2000), control of anxiety (Bale et al., 2001; Yoshida et al., 2009), and regulation of spatial memory (Tomizawa et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ferguson et al., 2001, 2000.

claim: Oxytocin controls anxiety.
source: Key regulatory effects of Oxt on animal and human behavior include promotion of facial recognition and maternal nurturing (Ferguson et al., 2001, 2000), control of anxiety (Bale et al., 2001; Yoshida et al., 2009), and regulation of spatial memory (Tomizawa et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bale et al., 2001; Yoshida et al., 2009.

claim: Oxytocin regulates spatial memory.
source: Key regulatory effects of Oxt on animal and human behavior include promotion of facial recognition and maternal nurturing (Ferguson et al., 2001, 2000), control of anxiety (Bale et al., 2001; Yoshida et al., 2009), and regulation of spatial memory (Tomizawa et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tomizawa et al., 2003.

claim: The behavioral phenotype of Oxtr knock-out mice recapitulates several symptoms of autism spectrum disorders (ASDs).
source: Notably, the behavioral phenotype of Oxtr knock-out (Oxtr−/−) mice recapitulates several symptoms of autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) (Lee et al., 2008; Sala et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2008; Sala et al., 2011.

claim: Behavioral changes in μ opiod receptor (Opmr1) knock-out mice are rescued upon Oxt administration.
source: Conversely, behavioral changes in mouse ASD models that are not based on direct perturbations of Oxt signaling, such as μ opiod receptor (Opmr1) (Gigliucci et al., 2014) or contactin associated protein-like 2 (Cntnap2) knock-outs (Peñagarikano et al., 2015), are rescued upon Oxt administration, and even human ASD patients improve with Oxt treatment (Andari et al., 2010; Hollander et al., 2007; Striepens et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gigliucci et al., 2014.

claim: Behavioral changes in contactin associated protein-like 2 (Cntnap2) knock-out mice are rescued upon Oxt administration.
source: Conversely, behavioral changes in mouse ASD models that are not based on direct perturbations of Oxt signaling, such as μ opiod receptor (Opmr1) (Gigliucci et al., 2014) or contactin associated protein-like 2 (Cntnap2) knock-outs (Peñagarikano et al., 2015), are rescued upon Oxt administration, and even human ASD patients improve with Oxt treatment (Andari et al., 2010; Hollander et al., 2007; Striepens et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Peñagarikano et al., 2015.

claim: Human ASD patients improve with Oxt treatment.
source: Conversely, behavioral changes in mouse ASD models that are not based on direct perturbations of Oxt signaling, such as μ opiod receptor (Opmr1) (Gigliucci et al., 2014) or contactin associated protein-like 2 (Cntnap2) knock-outs (Peñagarikano et al., 2015), are rescued upon Oxt administration, and even human ASD patients improve with Oxt treatment (Andari et al., 2010; Hollander et al., 2007; Striepens et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Andari et al., 2010; Hollander et al., 2007; Striepens et al., 2011.

claim: Oxtr polymorphisms have been linked with ASDs.
source: Moreover, Oxtr polymorphisms (LoParo and Waldman, 2015) and abnormal methylation of the Oxtr promoter (Elagoz Yuksel et al., 2016) have been linked with ASDs, supporting the notion that altered Oxt signaling can contribute to ASDs.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to LoParo and Waldman, 2015.

claim: Abnormal methylation of the Oxtr promoter has been linked with ASDs.
source: Moreover, Oxtr polymorphisms (LoParo and Waldman, 2015) and abnormal methylation of the Oxtr promoter (Elagoz Yuksel et al., 2016) have been linked with ASDs, supporting the notion that altered Oxt signaling can contribute to ASDs.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Elagoz Yuksel et al., 2016.

claim: Altered Oxt signaling can contribute to ASDs.
source: Moreover, Oxtr polymorphisms (LoParo and Waldman, 2015) and abnormal methylation of the Oxtr promoter (Elagoz Yuksel et al., 2016) have been linked with ASDs, supporting the notion that altered Oxt signaling can contribute to ASDs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cited evidence about Oxtr polymorphisms and methylation being linked to ASDs.

claim: An Oxt surge in the maternal bloodstream at delivery promotes labor and subsequent lactation.
source: At delivery, an Oxt surge in the maternal bloodstream promotes labor and subsequent lactation.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about oxytocin's role in parturition and lactation.

claim: Circulating Oxt reaches the fetal brain and regulates the developmental switch of GABAergic signaling from excitation to inhibition.
source: The circulating Oxt reaches the fetal brain, where it regulates the developmental switch of GABAergic signaling from excitation to inhibition (Tyzio et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tyzio et al., 2006.

claim: The developmental switch of GABAergic signaling from excitation to inhibition appears to be impaired in the valproate-intoxication mouse model of ASDs.
source: This switch appears to be impaired in the valproate-intoxication and fragile-X-syndrome mouse models of ASDs, and to be restored by Oxt treatment.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the statement about the switch being impaired in these models.

claim: The developmental switch of GABAergic signaling from excitation to inhibition appears to be impaired in the fragile-X-syndrome mouse model of ASDs.
source: This switch appears to be impaired in the valproate-intoxication and fragile-X-syndrome mouse models of ASDs, and to be restored by Oxt treatment.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the statement about the switch being impaired in these models.

claim: The impaired developmental switch of GABAergic signaling in valproate-intoxication and fragile-X-syndrome mouse models of ASDs is restored by Oxt treatment.
source: This switch appears to be impaired in the valproate-intoxication and fragile-X-syndrome mouse models of ASDs, and to be restored by Oxt treatment.
evidence: This claim is stated directly in the manuscript.

claim: Administration of an Oxtr antagonist to naïve pregnant mice one day before delivery leads to ASD-like features in the offspring.
source: Moreover, administration of an Oxtr antagonist to naïve pregnant mice one day before delivery leads to ASD-like features in the offspring (Tyzio et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tyzio et al., 2014.

claim: Early blockade of Oxt signaling affects the development of synaptic wiring in the brain and leads to lifelong consequences, including neuropsychiatric diseases.
source: These findings indicate that an early blockade of Oxt signaling affects the development of synaptic wiring in the brain and leads to lifelong consequences, including neuropsychiatric diseases.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the findings about Oxtr antagonist administration leading to ASD-like features.

claim: Oxtr−/− mice show an increased seizure propensity.
source: This notion is supported by the observations that Oxtr−/− mice show an increased seizure propensity and that the relative contribution of GABAergic synapses is reduced in cultured hippocampal Oxtr−/− neurons (Sala et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sala et al., 2011.

claim: The relative contribution of GABAergic synapses is reduced in cultured hippocampal Oxtr−/− neurons.
source: This notion is supported by the observations that Oxtr−/− mice show an increased seizure propensity and that the relative contribution of GABAergic synapses is reduced in cultured hippocampal Oxtr−/− neurons (Sala et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sala et al., 2011.

claim: Oxt exposure did not affect neuronal survival in hippocampal cultures.
source: Oxt exposure did not affect neuronal survival (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b) but reduced the dendritic arborization of neurons at 14 DIV, as assessed by Sholl analysis (Sholl, 1953) of cells stained with an antibody to the dendrite marker Map2 (Figure 1a–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: Oxt exposure reduced the dendritic arborization of neurons at 14 DIV.
source: Oxt exposure did not affect neuronal survival (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b) but reduced the dendritic arborization of neurons at 14 DIV, as assessed by Sholl analysis (Sholl, 1953) of cells stained with an antibody to the dendrite marker Map2 (Figure 1a–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1a–c and uses Sholl analysis methodology.

claim: Altered dendrite branching by Oxt was found only in wild-type glutamatergic neurons.
source: The altered dendrite branching was found only in wild-type (WT) glutamatergic neurons, but not in WT hippocampal inhibitory neurons identified by VGAT staining (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a,b) or in Oxtr-deficient neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a,b and Figure 1—figure supplement 3a–c.

claim: Altered dendrite branching by Oxt was not found in WT hippocampal inhibitory neurons identified by VGAT staining.
source: The altered dendrite branching was found only in wild-type (WT) glutamatergic neurons, but not in WT hippocampal inhibitory neurons identified by VGAT staining (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a,b) or in Oxtr-deficient neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a,b.

claim: Altered dendrite branching by Oxt was not found in Oxtr-deficient neurons.
source: The altered dendrite branching was found only in wild-type (WT) glutamatergic neurons, but not in WT hippocampal inhibitory neurons identified by VGAT staining (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a,b) or in Oxtr-deficient neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3a–c.

claim: Oxt exposure reduced the number of juxtaposed glutamatergic pre- and post-synaptic sites.
source: Oxt exposure reduced the number of juxtaposed glutamatergic pre- and post-synaptic sites, but no changes were detected in the spatial coincidence of pre- and postsynaptic labeling (Mander's overlapping coefficient) (Figure 1e–g), indicating that the integrity of the remaining glutamatergic synapses is maintained.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1e–g.

claim: No changes were detected in the spatial coincidence of pre- and postsynaptic labeling (Mander's overlapping coefficient) after Oxt exposure.
source: Oxt exposure reduced the number of juxtaposed glutamatergic pre- and post-synaptic sites, but no changes were detected in the spatial coincidence of pre- and postsynaptic labeling (Mander's overlapping coefficient) (Figure 1e–g), indicating that the integrity of the remaining glutamatergic synapses is maintained.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1e–g.

claim: The integrity of the remaining glutamatergic synapses is maintained after Oxt exposure.
source: Oxt exposure reduced the number of juxtaposed glutamatergic pre- and post-synaptic sites, but no changes were detected in the spatial coincidence of pre- and postsynaptic labeling (Mander's overlapping coefficient) (Figure 1e–g), indicating that the integrity of the remaining glutamatergic synapses is maintained.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing no changes in Mander's overlapping coefficient.

claim: ATO treatment abolished the Oxt-induced effects on dendrite arborization.
source: Morphological analyses at 14 DIV showed that ATO treatment abolished the Oxt-induced effects on dendrite arborization, whereas ATO alone was ineffective (Figure 1h–j), indicating that the Oxt effects on dendrites and synapses of hippocampal neurons are mediated by Oxtrs.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1h–j.

claim: ATO alone was ineffective on dendrite arborization.
source: Morphological analyses at 14 DIV showed that ATO treatment abolished the Oxt-induced effects on dendrite arborization, whereas ATO alone was ineffective (Figure 1h–j), indicating that the Oxt effects on dendrites and synapses of hippocampal neurons are mediated by Oxtrs.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1h–j.

claim: The Oxt effects on dendrites and synapses of hippocampal neurons are mediated by Oxtrs.
source: Morphological analyses at 14 DIV showed that ATO treatment abolished the Oxt-induced effects on dendrite arborization, whereas ATO alone was ineffective (Figure 1h–j), indicating that the Oxt effects on dendrites and synapses of hippocampal neurons are mediated by Oxtrs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing that ATO (an Oxtr antagonist) abolished Oxt effects.

claim: The amplitudes of evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) were decreased in Oxt-treated glutamatergic neurons.
source: The amplitudes of evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) were decreased in Oxt-treated glutamatergic neurons (Figure 2a,c).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2a,c.

claim: The size of the apparent readily releasable pool (RRP) of glutamatergic synaptic vesicles was decreased in Oxt-treated glutamatergic neurons.
source: The same was true for the size of the apparent readily releasable pool (RRP) of glutamatergic synaptic vesicles (SVs), as assessed by the EPSC induced by the application of a hypertonic sucrose solution (Nair et al., 2013; Rosenmund and Stevens, 1996) (Figure a,d).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2a,d and uses methodology from cited references.

claim: Neither evoked inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) amplitudes nor the RRP of GABAergic neurons were affected by Oxt.
source: In contrast, neither evoked inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) amplitudes nor the RRP of GABAergic neurons, which represent a minor cell fraction in hippocampal autaptic cultures, were affected by Oxt, indicating that Oxt exclusively acts on excitatory hippocampal neurons in culture (Figure 2b–d).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2b–d.

claim: Oxt exclusively acts on excitatory hippocampal neurons in culture.
source: In contrast, neither evoked inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) amplitudes nor the RRP of GABAergic neurons, which represent a minor cell fraction in hippocampal autaptic cultures, were affected by Oxt, indicating that Oxt exclusively acts on excitatory hippocampal neurons in culture (Figure 2b–d).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing differential effects on excitatory vs. inhibitory neurons.

claim: The vesicular release probability (Pvr) of glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons was not changed by Oxt exposure.
source: The vesicular release probability (Pvr) of glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons, calculated by dividing the postsynaptic charge transfer elicited by an action potential (AP) by the postsynaptic charge transfer in response to RRP release, was not changed by Oxt exposure (Figure 2e), indicating that the fusion-probability of primed SVs is not altered by Oxt.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The fusion-probability of primed SVs is not altered by Oxt.
source: The vesicular release probability (Pvr) of glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons, calculated by dividing the postsynaptic charge transfer elicited by an action potential (AP) by the postsynaptic charge transfer in response to RRP release, was not changed by Oxt exposure (Figure 2e), indicating that the fusion-probability of primed SVs is not altered by Oxt.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing no change in Pvr.

claim: EPSC and IPSC amplitudes depressed similarly during 10 Hz stimulus trains irrespective of Oxt-treatment.
source: We next studied synaptic short-term plasticity (STP) by measuring synaptic responses during 10 Hz stimulus trains, and found that EPSC and IPSC amplitudes depressed similarly and irrespective of Oxt-treatment (Figure 2l,m).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2l,m.

claim: Oxt specifically causes strong reductions of EPSCs but does not affect the fundamental characteristics of the presynaptic transmitter release machinery.
source: These findings indicate that Oxt specifically causes strong reductions of EPSCs but does not affect the fundamental characteristics of the presynaptic transmitter release machinery.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing reduced EPSCs but unchanged Pvr and short-term plasticity.

claim: Miniature EPSC (mEPSC) amplitudes were not affected by Oxt treatment.
source: Miniature EPSC (mEPSC) amplitudes were not affected by Oxt treatment, indicating that postsynaptic sensitivity to quantal release at single synapses is not affected by Oxt (Figure 2i,j).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2i,j.

claim: Postsynaptic sensitivity to quantal release at single synapses is not affected by Oxt.
source: Miniature EPSC (mEPSC) amplitudes were not affected by Oxt treatment, indicating that postsynaptic sensitivity to quantal release at single synapses is not affected by Oxt (Figure 2i,j).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing no change in mEPSC amplitudes.

claim: A significant reduction of mEPSC frequency was detected after Oxt treatment.
source: In contrast, we detected a significant reduction of mEPSC frequency, indicating that Oxt reduces the number of functional glutamatergic synapses (Figure 2k).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2k.

claim: Oxt reduces the number of functional glutamatergic synapses.
source: In contrast, we detected a significant reduction of mEPSC frequency, indicating that Oxt reduces the number of functional glutamatergic synapses (Figure 2k).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing reduced mEPSC frequency.

claim: mIPSC events in GABAergic neurons were not altered by Oxt.
source: Again, reflecting the morphological and IPSC data, mIPSC events in GABAergic neurons were not altered by Oxt (Figure 2i–k).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2i–k.

claim: GABA-induced currents were not changed in Oxt-treated GABAergic neurons.
source: Corroborating our PSC data, GABA-induced currents were not changed in Oxt-treated GABAergic neurons, whereas Oxt-exposed glutamatergic neurons showed a reduction of their responses to glutamate as compared to untreated cells (Figure 2f–h).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2f–h.

claim: Oxt-exposed glutamatergic neurons showed a reduction of their responses to glutamate as compared to untreated cells.
source: Corroborating our PSC data, GABA-induced currents were not changed in Oxt-treated GABAergic neurons, whereas Oxt-exposed glutamatergic neurons showed a reduction of their responses to glutamate as compared to untreated cells (Figure 2f–h).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2f–h.

claim: The number of surface glutamate receptors in glutamatergic neurons is decreased by early Oxt exposure.
source: This indicates that the number of surface glutamate receptors in glutamatergic neurons, but not of GABAA receptors in GABAergic cells, is decreased by early Oxt exposure, supporting the notion that Oxt specifically affects excitatory neurons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing reduced responses to glutamate.

claim: The number of surface GABAA receptors in GABAergic cells is not decreased by early Oxt exposure.
source: This indicates that the number of surface glutamate receptors in glutamatergic neurons, but not of GABAA receptors in GABAergic cells, is decreased by early Oxt exposure, supporting the notion that Oxt specifically affects excitatory neurons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing no change in GABA-induced currents.

claim: Oxt requires the Oxtr to exert its actions on neurons.
source: To exert these actions, Oxt requires the Oxtr, since the addition of ATO suppressed the reduction of EPSCs induced by Oxt (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–k) and Oxtr-deficient neurons did not show any changes in their electrophysiological characteristics upon Oxt treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 3d–j).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–k and Figure 1—figure supplement 3d–j.

claim: Oxt effects were restricted to the early phase of synaptic development.
source: Surprisingly, Oxt effects were restricted to the early phase of synaptic development, as Oxt-application to neurons from DIV 7 onwards, that is, at a time when synaptogenesis is ongoing, did not cause any changes in the morphology and function of glutamatergic neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a–k).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a–k.

claim: Oxt reduced dendrite complexity and synaptic transmission of glutamatergic neurons in E18 cultures.
source: As with P0 cultures (see above), Oxt reduced dendrite complexity and synaptic transmission of glutamatergic neurons in E18 cultures (Figure 2—figure supplement 3a–j) without impairing nerve cell survival (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3a–j and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: U73122 blocked all morphological and electrophysiological effects induced by Oxt.
source: To test which intracellular pathway mediates the Oxt-induced effects on glutamatergic neurons, we exposed hippocampal neurons to Oxt for 1 DIV in the presence of the PLCβ inhibitor U73122. U73122 blocked all morphological and electrophysiological effects induced by Oxt, whereas U73122 exposure alone was ineffective (Figure 2—figure supplement 4a–n).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4a–n.

claim: U73122 exposure alone was ineffective on neuronal morphology and electrophysiology.
source: To test which intracellular pathway mediates the Oxt-induced effects on glutamatergic neurons, we exposed hippocampal neurons to Oxt for 1 DIV in the presence of the PLCβ inhibitor U73122. U73122 blocked all morphological and electrophysiological effects induced by Oxt, whereas U73122 exposure alone was ineffective (Figure 2—figure supplement 4a–n).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4a–n.

claim: Oxt still partially exerted effects on glutamatergic neurons after cultures had been exposed to pertussis toxin (PTX).
source: Moreover, Oxt still partially exerted effects on glutamatergic neurons after cultures had been exposed from 1 DIV to 3 DIV to 100 ng/μl pertussis toxin (PTX), which blocks Gi/Go-signaling (Figure 2—figure supplement 5a–b).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5a–b.

claim: Oxtrs coupled to Gq/11 modulate hippocampal glutamatergic neurons.
source: These results indicate that Oxtrs coupled to Gq/11 modulate hippocampal glutamatergic neurons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing that PLCβ inhibition blocks Oxt effects while Gi/Go inhibition does not.

claim: Oxt exposure did not affect functional parameters of striatal neurons.
source: As seen for GABAergic hippocampal neurons, Oxt exposure did not affect functional (Figure 3a–g) or morphological parameters (Figure 3h,k) of striatal neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3a–g and Figure 3h,k.

claim: Oxt exposure did not affect morphological parameters of striatal neurons.
source: As seen for GABAergic hippocampal neurons, Oxt exposure did not affect functional (Figure 3a–g) or morphological parameters (Figure 3h,k) of striatal neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3h,k.

claim: Oxt did not alter the number of GABAergic synapses of striatal neurons.
source: Further, quantitative analyses of GABAergic pre- and postsynapses, as identified by immunolabeling of VGAT and Gephyrin, respectively (Nair et al., 2013), showed that Oxt did not alter the number of GABAergic synapses of striatal neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–c and uses methodology from cited reference.

claim: Oxt treatment for 1 or 3 DIV caused reductions of evoked IPSC amplitudes in Oxtr-overexpressing striatal cells.
source: Electrophysiological analyses of Oxtr-overexpressing cells, as identified via EGFP fluorescence, indicated that Oxt treatment for 1 or 3 DIV caused reductions of evoked IPSC amplitudes, of the RRP, and of the response to exogenous application of GABA, which was not seen in control cells expressing EGFP (Figure 3a–g).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3a–g.

claim: Oxt treatment for 1 or 3 DIV caused reductions of the RRP in Oxtr-overexpressing striatal cells.
source: Electrophysiological analyses of Oxtr-overexpressing cells, as identified via EGFP fluorescence, indicated that Oxt treatment for 1 or 3 DIV caused reductions of evoked IPSC amplitudes, of the RRP, and of the response to exogenous application of GABA, which was not seen in control cells expressing EGFP (Figure 3a–g).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3a–g.

claim: Oxt treatment for 1 or 3 DIV caused reductions of the response to exogenous application of GABA in Oxtr-overexpressing striatal cells.
source: Electrophysiological analyses of Oxtr-overexpressing cells, as identified via EGFP fluorescence, indicated that Oxt treatment for 1 or 3 DIV caused reductions of evoked IPSC amplitudes, of the RRP, and of the response to exogenous application of GABA, which was not seen in control cells expressing EGFP (Figure 3a–g).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3a–g.

claim: The Pvr was not affected by Oxt in Oxtr-overexpressing striatal cells.
source: The Pvr was not affected (Figure 3f).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3f.

claim: Following early Oxt exposure, Oxtr-overexpressing GABAergic neurons developed less dendritic arborizations than cells expressing only EGFP.
source: Following early Oxt exposure, Oxtr-overexpressing GABAergic neurons developed less dendritic arborizations than cells expressing only EGFP (Figure 3i–k).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3i–k.

claim: Striatal GABAergic neurons are insensitive to Oxt because they lack Oxtrs.
source: These data indicate that striatal GABAergic neurons are insensitive to Oxt because they lack Oxtrs, but can be rendered Oxt-sensitive upon ectopic expression of Oxtrs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing that Oxtr overexpression renders striatal neurons sensitive to Oxt.

claim: Striatal GABAergic neurons can be rendered Oxt-sensitive upon ectopic expression of Oxtrs.
source: These data indicate that striatal GABAergic neurons are insensitive to Oxt because they lack Oxtrs, but can be rendered Oxt-sensitive upon ectopic expression of Oxtrs.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing that Oxtr overexpression renders striatal neurons sensitive to Oxt.

claim: Venus is expressed in mouse hippocampus in OxtrVn/+ mice.
source: As reported (Yoshida et al., 2009), we found Venus to be expressed in mouse hippocampus (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,c,d), while no expression was detected in the striatum (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,c,d and corroborated by citation to Yoshida et al., 2009.

claim: No Venus expression was detected in the striatum in OxtrVn/+ mice.
source: As reported (Yoshida et al., 2009), we found Venus to be expressed in mouse hippocampus (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,c,d), while no expression was detected in the striatum (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Venus expression was detectable in the hippocampus at different developmental stages (P3, P5, P10, 3W and 13W).
source: Venus expression was detectable in the hippocampus at different developmental stages (P3, P5, P10, 3W and 13W; data not shown).
evidence: This claim is stated but data is not shown in the manuscript.

claim: Venus signal was detected within the entire hippocampus (i.e. rostral, medial, and caudal) and across all subcompartments (e.g. CA1, CA3, and DG).
source: Venus signal was detected within the entire hippocampus (i.e. rostral, medial, and caudal) and across all subcompartments (e.g. CA1, CA3, and DG).
evidence: This claim is stated directly in the manuscript.

claim: Venus-expressing cells were positive for the neuron-specific nuclear protein (NeuN) and Map2, indicating their neuronal identity.
source: Venus-expressing cells were also positive for the neuron-specific nuclear protein (NeuN) and Map2, indicating their neuronal identity (Figure 4a,c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1c,d).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4a,c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1c,d.

claim: No Oxtr expression was detected in astrocytes in brain slices immunostained for Venus and the astrocytic marker S100.
source: No Oxtr expression was detected in astrocytes in brain slices immunostained for Venus and the astrocytic marker S100 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a,b), and in contrast to whole brain samples, no Oxtr gene expression was detected in primary cultured OxtrVn/Vn astrocytes as assessed by Western blotting for Venus (Figure 4—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2a,b.

claim: No Oxtr gene expression was detected in primary cultured OxtrVn/Vn astrocytes as assessed by Western blotting for Venus.
source: No Oxtr expression was detected in astrocytes in brain slices immunostained for Venus and the astrocytic marker S100 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a,b), and in contrast to whole brain samples, no Oxtr gene expression was detected in primary cultured OxtrVn/Vn astrocytes as assessed by Western blotting for Venus (Figure 4—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2c.

claim: Only 16% of the total GAD-positive neurons in hippocampal slices express Venus.
source: Quantitative analyses of neurons positive for Venus and GAD67 showed that only 16% of the total GAD-positive neurons in slices express Venus (Figure 4b,c).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4b,c.

claim: Only a very small subpopulation of GABAergic cells (19%) express Oxtr.
source: Quantitative analysis of neurons positive for Oxtr-Venus and GABA showed that only a very small subpopulation of GABAergic cells (19%) express Oxtr (Figure 4b,d).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4b,d.

claim: The density of VGAT-positive puncta was reduced in Oxtr−/− cultures as compared to Oxtr+/+ cultures.
source: Quantitative analyses of VGAT- or VGLUT1-positive fluorescent puncta juxtaposed to Map2-positive dendrites showed that the density of VGAT-positive puncta was reduced and the density of VGLUT1-positive puncta was increased in Oxtr−/− cultures as compared to Oxtr+/+ cultures (Figure 5a,c).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5a,c.

claim: The density of VGLUT1-positive puncta was increased in Oxtr−/− cultures as compared to Oxtr+/+ cultures.
source: Quantitative analyses of VGAT- or VGLUT1-positive fluorescent puncta juxtaposed to Map2-positive dendrites showed that the density of VGAT-positive puncta was reduced and the density of VGLUT1-positive puncta was increased in Oxtr−/− cultures as compared to Oxtr+/+ cultures (Figure 5a,c).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5a,c.

claim: The imbalance in excitation/inhibition in Oxtr−/− cultures appears to be caused by altered synapse numbers rather than a change in the ratio between excitatory and inhibitory neurons.
source: This imbalance appears to be caused by altered synapse numbers rather than a change in the ratio between excitatory and inhibitory neurons, because the number of GAD65/67-positive GABAergic neurons was similar in Oxtr−/− and Oxtr+/+ cultures (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing similar numbers of GABAergic neurons in both genotypes.

claim: The number of GAD65/67-positive GABAergic neurons was similar in Oxtr−/− and Oxtr+/+ cultures.
source: This imbalance appears to be caused by altered synapse numbers rather than a change in the ratio between excitatory and inhibitory neurons, because the number of GAD65/67-positive GABAergic neurons was similar in Oxtr−/− and Oxtr+/+ cultures (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: The number of parvalbumin-positive cells was similar in hippocampal cultures of Oxtr−/− vs. Oxtr+/+ mice.
source: Likewise, the number of parvalbumin-positive cells, a sub-population of inhibitory interneurons, was similar in hippocampal cultures (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c,d) and brain slices (Figure 5—figure supplement 1e,f) of Oxtr−/− vs. Oxtr+/+ mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1c,d.

claim: The number of parvalbumin-positive cells was similar in brain slices of Oxtr−/− vs. Oxtr+/+ mice.
source: Likewise, the number of parvalbumin-positive cells, a sub-population of inhibitory interneurons, was similar in hippocampal cultures (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c,d) and brain slices (Figure 5—figure supplement 1e,f) of Oxtr−/− vs. Oxtr+/+ mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1e,f.

claim: The number of excitatory presynapses is increased in cultures from Oxtr−/− mice.
source: These data indicate that the number of excitatory presynapses is increased in cultures from Oxtr−/− mice whereas the number of inhibitory presynapses is slightly decreased.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing increased VGLUT1-positive puncta.

claim: The number of inhibitory presynapses is slightly decreased in cultures from Oxtr−/− mice.
source: These data indicate that the number of excitatory presynapses is increased in cultures from Oxtr−/− mice whereas the number of inhibitory presynapses is slightly decreased.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing reduced VGAT-positive puncta.

claim: Oxtr−/− neurons at 14 DIV exhibited an increase of the density of NL1-positive clusters as compared to Oxtr+/+ neurons.
source: As compared to Oxtr+/+ neurons, Oxtr−/− neurons at 14 DIV exhibited an increase of the density of NL1-positive clusters, a decrease of the density of NL2-positive clusters, an increase in the number of excitatory synaptic structures with partially colocalized Synaptophysin and PSD95, and a decrease in the number of inhibitory synaptic structures with partially colocalized Synaptophysin and Gephyrin (Figure 5d–g).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5d–g.

claim: Oxtr−/− neurons at 14 DIV exhibited a decrease of the density of NL2-positive clusters as compared to Oxtr+/+ neurons.
source: As compared to Oxtr+/+ neurons, Oxtr−/− neurons at 14 DIV exhibited an increase of the density of NL1-positive clusters, a decrease of the density of NL2-positive clusters, an increase in the number of excitatory synaptic structures with partially colocalized Synaptophysin and PSD95, and a decrease in the number of inhibitory synaptic structures with partially colocalized Synaptophysin and Gephyrin (Figure 5d–g).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5d–g.

claim: Oxtr−/− neurons at 14 DIV exhibited an increase in the number of excitatory synaptic structures with partially colocalized Synaptophysin and PSD95 as compared to Oxtr+/+ neurons.
source: As compared to Oxtr+/+ neurons, Oxtr−/− neurons at 14 DIV exhibited an increase of the density of NL1-positive clusters, a decrease of the density of NL2-positive clusters, an increase in the number of excitatory synaptic structures with partially colocalized Synaptophysin and PSD95, and a decrease in the number of inhibitory synaptic structures with partially colocalized Synaptophysin and Gephyrin (Figure 5d–g).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5d–g.

claim: Oxtr−/− neurons at 14 DIV exhibited a decrease in the number of inhibitory synaptic structures with partially colocalized Synaptophysin and Gephyrin as compared to Oxtr+/+ neurons.
source: As compared to Oxtr+/+ neurons, Oxtr−/− neurons at 14 DIV exhibited an increase of the density of NL1-positive clusters, a decrease of the density of NL2-positive clusters, an increase in the number of excitatory synaptic structures with partially colocalized Synaptophysin and PSD95, and a decrease in the number of inhibitory synaptic structures with partially colocalized Synaptophysin and Gephyrin (Figure 5d–g).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5d–g.

claim: The number of GluA1-positive clusters was increased in Oxtr−/− cultures.
source: Further, the number of GluA1-positive clusters was increased in Oxtr−/− cultures, whereas no differences were detected for GABAAγ2 (Figure 5d–g).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5d–g.

claim: No differences were detected for GABAAγ2 in Oxtr−/− cultures compared to Oxtr+/+ cultures.
source: Further, the number of GluA1-positive clusters was increased in Oxtr−/− cultures, whereas no differences were detected for GABAAγ2 (Figure 5d–g).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5d–g.

claim: The ratio between excitatory and inhibitory synapses is shifted towards increased excitation in mass cultures of hippocampal neurons lacking Oxtrs.
source: These data again indicate that the ratio between excitatory and inhibitory synapses is shifted towards increased excitation in mass cultures of hippocampal neurons lacking Oxtrs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing increased excitatory and decreased inhibitory synapse markers.

claim: The frequency and amplitude of sEPSCs were increased in Oxtr−/− cultures.
source: The frequency and amplitude of sEPSCs were increased in Oxtr−/− cultures (Figure 5h,j,k), while no differences in sIPSC events were detected (Figure 5i,l,m).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5h,j,k.

claim: No differences in sIPSC events were detected in Oxtr−/− cultures compared to Oxtr+/+ cultures.
source: The frequency and amplitude of sEPSCs were increased in Oxtr−/− cultures (Figure 5h,j,k), while no differences in sIPSC events were detected (Figure 5i,l,m).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5i,l,m.

claim: The increase in the number of apparent glutamatergic synapses is paralleled by an increase in glutamatergic synaptic activity in Oxtr−/− cultures as compared to Oxtr+/+ cultures.
source: Thus, the increase in the number of apparent glutamatergic synapses, as assessed by immunofluorescence staining, is paralleled by an increase in glutamatergic synaptic activity in Oxtr−/− cultures as compared to Oxtr+/+ cultures.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing both increased synapse markers and increased sEPSC frequency/amplitude.

claim: TGOT caused an increase in the number of VGAT- and NL2-positive structures in primary hippocampal neurons in mass culture.
source: TGOT caused an increase in the number of VGAT- and NL2-positive structures, and a decrease of the number of VGLUT1- and NL1-positive structures (Figure 5—figure supplement 2a–d).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2a–d.

claim: TGOT caused a decrease of the number of VGLUT1- and NL1-positive structures in primary hippocampal neurons in mass culture.
source: TGOT caused an increase in the number of VGAT- and NL2-positive structures, and a decrease of the number of VGLUT1- and NL1-positive structures (Figure 5—figure supplement 2a–d).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2a–d.

claim: TGOT treatment was paralleled by a decrease in glutamatergic transmission, as indicated by reduced sEPSC amplitudes and frequencies.
source: This was paralleled by a decrease in glutamatergic transmission, as indicated by reduced sEPSC amplitudes and frequencies upon TGOT treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 2e–g).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2e–g.

claim: Early activation of Oxtr in hippocampal neurons shifts the synaptic excitation/inhibition balance towards reduced excitation.
source: These data again indicate that the early activation of Oxtr in hippocampal neurons shifts the synaptic excitation/inhibition balance towards reduced excitation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing TGOT effects on synapse markers and transmission.

claim: OxtrVn/Vn pyramidal neurons exhibited a more pronounced dendrite complexity at the apical and basal poles as compared to control cells.
source: OxtrVn/Vn pyramidal neurons exhibited a more pronounced dendrite complexity at the apical and basal poles as compared to control cells (Figure 6a), with an increased number of primary apical dendrite branches and of basal primary neurites, but no changes in the apical shaft length (Figure 6b–d).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: OxtrVn/Vn pyramidal neurons had an increased number of primary apical dendrite branches.
source: OxtrVn/Vn pyramidal neurons exhibited a more pronounced dendrite complexity at the apical and basal poles as compared to control cells (Figure 6a), with an increased number of primary apical dendrite branches and of basal primary neurites, but no changes in the apical shaft length (Figure 6b–d).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6b–d.

claim: OxtrVn/Vn pyramidal neurons had an increased number of basal primary neurites.
source: OxtrVn/Vn pyramidal neurons exhibited a more pronounced dendrite complexity at the apical and basal poles as compared to control cells (Figure 6a), with an increased number of primary apical dendrite branches and of basal primary neurites, but no changes in the apical shaft length (Figure 6b–d).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6b–d.

claim: No changes in the apical shaft length were observed in OxtrVn/Vn pyramidal neurons.
source: OxtrVn/Vn pyramidal neurons exhibited a more pronounced dendrite complexity at the apical and basal poles as compared to control cells (Figure 6a), with an increased number of primary apical dendrite branches and of basal primary neurites, but no changes in the apical shaft length (Figure 6b–d).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6b–d.

claim: An increased density of filopodia and filopodia-like protrusions along the apical dendrite shafts of OxtrVn/Vn neurons was detected as compared to Oxtr+/+ cells.
source: We also detected an increased density of filopodia and filopodia-like protrusions along the apical dendrite shafts of OxtrVn/Vn neurons as compared to Oxtr+/+ cells (Figure 6e).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6e.

claim: A similarly enhanced dendrite complexity was observed in OxtrVn/Vn pyramidal neurons in CA3.
source: A similarly enhanced dendrite complexity was observed in OxtrVn/Vn pyramidal neurons in CA3 (Figure 6f,g).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6f,g.

claim: Oxt signaling is required in vivo to control the morphology of hippocampal pyramidal cells.
source: These data indicate that Oxt signaling is required in vivo to control the morphology of hippocampal pyramidal cells, in line with the findings on hippocampal neuron cultures that mainly contain pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing altered morphology in OxtrVn/Vn neurons.

claim: An increase of the mEPSC frequency but not of mEPSC amplitudes was detected in OxtrVn/Vn CA1 and CA3 pyramidal neurons.
source: We detected an increase of the mEPSC frequency but not of mEPSC amplitudes in OxtrVn/Vn CA1 and CA3 pyramidal neurons (Figure 7a–c), while mIPSC events were unchanged (Figure 7d–f).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7a–c.

claim: mIPSC events were unchanged in OxtrVn/Vn CA1 and CA3 pyramidal neurons.
source: We detected an increase of the mEPSC frequency but not of mEPSC amplitudes in OxtrVn/Vn CA1 and CA3 pyramidal neurons (Figure 7a–c), while mIPSC events were unchanged (Figure 7d–f).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7d–f.

claim: A significant increase in dendritic branching points was detected in CA1 and CA3 OxtrVn/Vn neurons.
source: We detected, as with the in utero electroporation experiments, a significant increase in dendritic branching points in CA1 and CA3 OxtrVn/Vn neurons (Figure 8c–j), indicating an increased dendrite complexity.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8c–j.

claim: Changes in dendritic branching were more pronounced in CA3 than in CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: These changes were more pronounced in CA3 than in CA1 pyramidal neurons and were paralleled by a larger number of total dendritic spines, particularly in basal dendrites (Figure 8k–m), where the additional spines were predominantly of the thin and mushroom type (Figure 8n–o).
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison of data in Figure 8.

claim: Changes in dendritic branching were paralleled by a larger number of total dendritic spines, particularly in basal dendrites.
source: These changes were more pronounced in CA3 than in CA1 pyramidal neurons and were paralleled by a larger number of total dendritic spines, particularly in basal dendrites (Figure 8k–m), where the additional spines were predominantly of the thin and mushroom type (Figure 8n–o).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8k–m.

claim: The additional spines in basal dendrites were predominantly of the thin and mushroom type.
source: These changes were more pronounced in CA3 than in CA1 pyramidal neurons and were paralleled by a larger number of total dendritic spines, particularly in basal dendrites (Figure 8k–m), where the additional spines were predominantly of the thin and mushroom type (Figure 8n–o).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8n–o.

claim: No differences in spine density were found in apical and basal dendrites of OxtrVn/Vn neurons.
source: No differences in spine density were found in apical and basal dendrites (Figure 8m).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8m.

claim: A reduced maximum and average power of γ-oscillations was found in OxtrVn/Vn slices as compared to Oxtr+/+ slices.
source: We stimulated brain slices with 100 nM kainate, analyzed the oscillatory activity at 25–45 Hz (Figure 6h), and found a reduced maximum and average power of γ-oscillations in OxtrVn/Vn slices as compared to Oxtr+/+ slices (Figure 6i,j), without changes in γ-oscillation frequencies.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7g–j (note: text refers to Figure 6 but should be Figure 7 based on figure order).

claim: No changes in γ-oscillation frequencies were found in OxtrVn/Vn slices as compared to Oxtr+/+ slices.
source: We stimulated brain slices with 100 nM kainate, analyzed the oscillatory activity at 25–45 Hz (Figure 6h), and found a reduced maximum and average power of γ-oscillations in OxtrVn/Vn slices as compared to Oxtr+/+ slices (Figure 6i,j), without changes in γ-oscillation frequencies.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7g–j (note: text refers to Figure 6 but should be Figure 7 based on figure order).

claim: A perturbation of Oxt signaling in the hippocampus leads to an aberrant development of pyramidal neurons that causes altered γ-oscillations.
source: These findings are compatible with the altered balance between synaptic excitation and inhibition in OxtrVn/Vn mice and show that a perturbation of Oxt signaling in the hippocampus leads to an aberrant development of pyramidal neurons that, in turn, causes altered γ- oscillations.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing both morphological changes and altered γ-oscillations.
